title: Earth & Weather
description: Earth science: weather and seasons, rocks and soils, the water cycle, India's monsoon, volcanoes and earthquakes, the layered Earth and plate tectonics, and climate. Children observe local weather and landforms before learning global systems.

lessons.title: What Is the Weather Today?
objectives: Name and describe different kinds of weather
Choose suitable clothes for the weather
prerequisites: Can describe what they see outside
explanation: Weather is what the air outside is like today. It might be sunny and hot, cloudy and grey, rainy and wet, or windy with leaves blowing around.
Weather changes from day to day and even during one day. The morning can be sunny and the afternoon rainy!
We dress for the weather: a hat and water bottle when it's sunny, a raincoat and umbrella when it's rainy, a sweater when it's cold.

lessons.title: Summer, Monsoon and Winter
objectives: Name the main seasons in India
Describe what changes in each season
explanation: A year has seasons — times when the weather is different. In much of India, there is a hot summer, a rainy monsoon, and a cooler winter.
In summer it is hot and sunny; mangoes are in season! In the monsoon, heavy rains fill rivers and make everything green. In winter, mornings are cool and we wear sweaters.
Many traditional calendars in India describe six seasons, called ritus, including spring and autumn.

context.text: Traditional Indian calendars name six ritus: Vasanta (spring), Grishma (summer), Varsha (monsoon), Sharad (autumn), Hemanta (pre-winter) and Shishira (winter).

lessons.title: Rock and Soil Detectives
objectives: Describe rocks by colour, texture and hardness
Describe what soil is made of
explanation: Rocks are natural, hard materials that make up the ground and mountains. Some are smooth like river pebbles, some rough like granite, some soft enough to scratch like chalk.
Soil is made of tiny bits of broken rock mixed with rotting plants and animals (called humus), water and air.
Soil is home to worms, insects and roots. Worms help by mixing the soil and letting air in.

story.text: Tara dug a little hole in the garden. A wriggly earthworm popped out. "Welcome to my kingdom!" it said. "I eat old leaves and mix the soil. My tunnels let air and water reach the roots." Tara gently covered it up again.

units.title: Where Does Rain Come From?
units.summary: Water goes round and round in the water cycle.

lessons.title: The Never-Ending Water Journey
objectives: Explain that rain falls from clouds
Describe the water cycle in simple steps
explanation: The Sun warms water in seas, rivers and lakes. Some of it turns into an invisible gas called water vapour and rises into the sky. This is evaporation.
High up, the air is cold. The water vapour cools into tiny droplets that make clouds. This is condensation.
When droplets join and get heavy, they fall as rain. The rain flows back into rivers and seas — and the journey starts again. That's the water cycle.

vocabulary.meaning: water moving from earth to sky and back again
many tiny water droplets in the sky
turn from liquid into gas
water falling from clouds

examples: The same water has been going round for millions of years.
Puddles dry up as water evaporates.

story.title: Droplet's Adventure
story.text: A little water droplet named Bindu lived in the sea. One hot day, the Sun warmed her and up she floated, light as a feather. High in the sky, she met other droplets and they huddled into a fluffy cloud. When the cloud got heavy, down Bindu fell as rain — into a river that carried her all the way home to the sea.

lessons.title: Landforms of India
objectives: Name and describe major landforms
Locate major Indian landforms
explanation: Landforms are the natural shapes of the land. Mountains are very high land; the Himalayas in the north of India contain the world's highest peaks, including Mount Everest on the Nepal–China border.
A plateau is high, flat land — like the Deccan Plateau in southern India. Plains are large, flat, low land, often by rivers — like the Gangetic Plain, with rich soil for farming.
A desert gets very little rain — like the Thar Desert in Rajasthan. An island has water all around it — like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

vocabulary.meaning: a natural shape of the land
high, flat land
low, flat land
a very dry place with little rain

examples: Southern India is a peninsula: sea on three sides.
Rivers carve valleys between mountains.

story.title: Kiko's Journey Across India
story.text: Kiko the mountain goat started in the snowy Himalayas, trotted down into the green Gangetic Plain, crossed the dry Thar Desert, climbed onto the Deccan Plateau, and finally saw the sea all around the southern tip of India. "Every landform has its own animals, plants and people," Kiko said.

lessons.title: How the Monsoon Comes
objectives: Explain in simple terms why the monsoon happens
Measure rainfall with a rain gauge
explanation: In summer, the land heats up faster than the sea. Warm air over the land rises, and cooler, moist air from the Indian Ocean flows in to replace it. These seasonal winds are the southwest monsoon.
The moist sea air rises over land and hills, cools, and drops heavy rain. The monsoon usually reaches Kerala around early June and spreads across India over the following weeks.
Most of India's yearly rain falls in the monsoon months. Farmers depend on it for crops, and it refills rivers, lakes and groundwater.

context.text: The India Meteorological Department tracks the monsoon's onset; the normal onset date over Kerala is around 1 June, though it varies by several days each year.

air full of moisture
a tool for measuring rainfall

examples: Cherrapunji and Mawsynram in Meghalaya are among the wettest places on Earth.

lessons.title: Volcanoes and Earthquakes
objectives: Describe the layers of the Earth
Explain what causes volcanoes and earthquakes and how to stay safe
explanation: The Earth has layers: a thin rocky crust (where we live), a thick hot mantle of rock that flows very slowly, and a very hot core of iron and nickel at the centre.
The crust is broken into giant pieces called plates that move a few centimetres a year. Where plates meet, pressure builds and is released suddenly as an earthquake.

At some plate edges and hot spots, melted rock (magma) rises through cracks. When it erupts at the surface it is called lava, building volcanoes. India's Barren Island in the Andaman Sea has an active volcano.

vocabulary.meaning: Earth's outer layer
the hot, slowly flowing layer under the crust
melted rock underground

examples: The Himalayas are still rising slowly as the Indian plate pushes into the Eurasian plate.

story.title: The Cracked Egg Earth
story.text: Nova boiled an egg and tapped it gently so the shell cracked into pieces. "The shell is like the crust, cracked into plates," Nova said. "The white is like the mantle, and the yolk is the core." Pressing the shell pieces together, Nova showed how they could crumple and push up — like mountains forming.

lessons.title: Three Families of Rocks
objectives: Classify rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic
Explain weathering and erosion
explanation: Igneous rocks form when magma or lava cools and hardens — like granite and basalt. The Deccan Traps are vast layers of basalt from ancient lava flows.
Sedimentary rocks form from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together over long periods — like sandstone and limestone. Fossils are usually found in sedimentary rocks.

Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change existing rocks — limestone becomes marble (like the Makrana marble of the Taj Mahal). Weathering breaks rocks down, and erosion carries the pieces away by water, wind and ice.

context.text: The Deccan Traps formed from enormous volcanic eruptions about 66 million years ago, around the time of the dinosaur extinction; scientists continue to research their role.

vocabulary.meaning: rock formed from cooled magma or lava

examples: Red sandstone of many Mughal forts is sedimentary.

story.title: The Marble's Long Story
story.text: A tiny sea shell sank to the ocean floor millions of years ago. Layer upon layer covered it, pressing it into limestone. Much later, deep heat and pressure squeezed the limestone into gleaming marble. Quarried and carved, it became part of a beautiful monument visited by millions.

lessons.title: Weather Is Not Climate
objectives: Distinguish weather from climate
Explain factors that affect climate
explanation: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular time and place — today's rain. Climate is the average weather pattern over many years, usually 30 or more.

Climate depends on latitude (places near the equator receive more direct sunlight), altitude (higher places are cooler — think of Shimla vs Delhi), and distance from the sea (coasts have milder temperatures).
India has many climates: the cold desert of Ladakh, the hot desert of Thar, the humid tropics of Kerala and the alpine Himalayas.

vocabulary.meaning: atmospheric conditions at a particular time
long-term average weather patterns

height above sea level

examples: A cold day in Chennai is weather; Chennai's tropical climate is long-term.
Shimla is cooler than Delhi in summer mainly because of altitude.

story.title: One Snowy Day
story.text: A rare cold wave brought frost to a city usually warm in winter. "So much for the climate getting warmer!" said someone. A scientist explained gently, "One cold day is weather. Climate is what the records show over decades."

lessons.title: Cyclones and Staying Safe
objectives: Explain how tropical cyclones form
Describe how early warnings and preparedness save lives
prerequisites: Knows the water cycle and winds
explanation: Tropical cyclones form over warm ocean water. Warm, moist air rises, cools and forms huge clouds, releasing energy that drives powerful spiralling winds around a calm centre called the eye.
Cyclones bring strong winds, very heavy rain, and storm surges — sea water pushed onto land. India's east coast, along the Bay of Bengal, is often affected.

Early warnings from weather services, cyclone shelters and evacuation plans have greatly reduced deaths. Odisha's preparedness is widely cited: deaths from severe cyclones in recent years have been far lower than in the 1999 super cyclone.

context.text: The 1999 Odisha super cyclone killed roughly 10,000 people. When Cyclone Phailin struck in 2013, large-scale evacuation of around a million people helped keep deaths to a few dozen, according to official and international reports.

vocabulary.meaning: a large spinning storm over warm ocean water

examples: Cyclone warnings use colour-coded alerts.

lessons.title: From Drift to Plate Tectonics
objectives: Evaluate evidence for continental drift and plate tectonics
Describe types of plate boundaries
explanation: In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that continents had drifted apart. His evidence: the matching shapes of coastlines, identical fossils (like the reptile Mesosaurus) on continents now separated by oceans, and matching rock layers.

Many scientists rejected the idea because Wegener could not explain how continents moved. In the 1950s–60s, mapping of the ocean floor revealed mid-ocean ridges and symmetrical magnetic stripes — evidence of sea-floor spreading.

Plate tectonics now explains this: at divergent boundaries plates move apart; at convergent boundaries they collide (forming mountains or subduction zones); at transform boundaries they slide past each other.

context.text: India was once part of the supercontinent Gondwana. Fossils of the seed fern Glossopteris occur in India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica.

vocabulary.meaning: the idea that continents move

an ancient southern supercontinent

examples: Himalayas: convergent boundary.
Mid-Atlantic Ridge: divergent boundary.

story.title: The Idea Ahead of Its Time
story.text: Alfred Wegener spent years gathering evidence that continents had moved. Critics mocked him for lacking a mechanism. He died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. Decades later, ocean-floor discoveries confirmed much of his idea — a reminder that science changes its mind when the evidence demands it.

lessons.title: The Greenhouse Effect
objectives: Explain the natural and enhanced greenhouse effect
Evaluate evidence for human-caused climate change
explanation: Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which gives off infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane and water vapour absorb some of this and warm the atmosphere. Without this natural greenhouse effect, Earth would be far too cold for most life.
Burning fossil fuels and cutting forests have increased CO₂ from about 280 parts per million before industrialisation to over 420 ppm today. This enhances the greenhouse effect.

Evidence of warming includes global temperature records, shrinking glaciers and sea ice, rising sea levels and ice-core records. Responses include mitigation (reducing emissions) and adaptation (preparing for changes).

context.text: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) concludes that human influence has unequivocally warmed the climate; global surface temperature has risen by roughly 1.1–1.2 °C since the late 1800s.

vocabulary.meaning: warming of Earth by gases trapping infrared radiation
coal, oil or gas formed from ancient organisms
reducing the causes of climate change

examples: Himalayan glaciers feeding rivers like the Ganga are retreating.

story.title: The Keeling Curve
story.text: In 1958, scientist Charles David Keeling began measuring CO₂ at Mauna Loa in Hawai'i. The line wiggled up and down with the seasons as plants grew and decayed — but year after year, it kept climbing. That simple, careful measurement became one of the most important graphs in science.
